PREFA  CE. 


In  this  second  volume  the  Poleynical  Tracts  of  Wiclif  against 
the  Sects  are  continued  and  brought  to  a  close,  heing  followed  hy  the 
Tracts  against  the  Pope. 

Ounng  to  the  circumstance  that  ,the  Oerman  Edition  in  one  vo- 
lume  was  printed  first,  the  paging  is  carried  on  in  this  second 
volume  where  the  first  broke  off.  References,  therefore,  may  he  to  the 
pages  of  either.  The  Indices  given  on  pages  715 — 840  comprehend 
the  matter  printed  in  both  volumes. 

As  this  very  moment  whilst  correcting  this  last  sheet,  there  comes 
under  my  notice  a  new  puhlication  on  the  relation  of  John  Hus  to 
John  Wiclif  (Hu^  und  Wiclif.  Zur  Oenesis  der  husitischen  Lehre. 
Von  Dr.  Johann  Loserth,  ord.  Prof.  der  Oeschichte  an  der  Univer- 
sitdt  %M  Czernowitz.  Prag,  Tempsky  und  Leipzig,  Freytag,  1884. 
X.  314  pp). 

To  it  I  would  draw  the  attention  of  my  readers.  The  Author, 
Dr.  Loserth,  shows,  that  the  whole  Husite  movement  is  nothing  more 
or  less  than  a  Bohemian  Wiclifism.  As  he  puts  in  on  pages  1 — 2, 
the  'name  af  Wiclif  was  for  many  years  the  banner  u/nder  which  a 
powerful  party  in  Bohemia  strove  and  struggled.^  He  even  goes  so 
far  as  to  say  that    ^Hus  owes  to    Wiclif  nearly   the   whole  of  his 


IV  PEJEFACB. 

theology   as  set  forth   in   his  Latin  Tracts^    and   that   'it  was   in 
upholding   Wiclifs  teaehing  Hus  lost  his  life.'' 

And  not  only  does  the  Author  ^nake  these  statements  —  he  proves 
hi.-i  assertions  in  their  minutest  details  (comp.  page  161  ff.,  and  Vol.  I 
of  the  present  edition  p.  XIII). 

Dresden,    Vitzthum  Oymnasium :  Ociober  31,  1883. 

Mudolf  JBuddensieg,  Lh\

the  Mss.,  I  have  to  confine  myself  to  a  few  short  notices.

J.  Division. 

Thesis:  the  prelates  of  the  English  Church  are  full  of  sins 
against  the  Holy  Trinity,  cap.  I; 

(1)  against  the  omnipotence  of  the  Father,  cap.  I 

(2)  against  the  wisdom  of  the  Son,  cap.  II 

(3)  against   the  goodness   and   charity    of  the  Holy   Ghost, 
cap.  III. 

(Purpose  of  tJie  Tract  is  to  induce  the  temporal  Lords  and  the 
people  to  make  an  end  to  the  enGroachments  of  the  rich  heneficed  clergy.) 

II.  Summary  of  its  Contents. 

Chap,  L  The  Author  begins  his  argumentation  hy  alluding  to  the 
doctrine  of  the  Holy  Trinity,  which  is  more  and  more  neglected,  p.  41 7 — 
418.  Nohody  is  allowed  to  sin  against  the  omnipotence  of  the  Father, 
urUess  he  is  punished  for  his  wrongdoings,  p.  419.  In  England  espe- 
daUy  there  is,  at  present,  much  offence  given  hy  ihe  rich  clergy  who 
in  more  than  one  point  sin  against  God^s  law.  For  their  wealth  and 
worldliness  is  (1)  against  the  will  of  Ood;  (2)  through  it  they  neglect 
nr  ministry,  and  thus  (3)  they  are  ruinous  to  the  welfare  of  the 
realm,  p.  419.  The  only  remedy  against  this  unhealtly  state,  is  to 
return  to  the  simple  Sect  of  Christ,  p.  419. 

Chap.  11.  Likewise  the  clergy  is  in  sin  against  the  Son,  the 
etemal  unsdom;  for  their  life  is  not  according  to  the  law  of  Christ, 
p.  420,  and  through  their  wealth  and  luxury  they  take  away  from 
the  poor  people,    the  hasis  of  the  realm,  what  is  necessary   to  them,

p.  421.     From  suddike  op^wession    the   ruin    of  the  land  is  not  far' 
off.     Remedy  against  this,  p.  422.^ 

Chap.  III.  If  they  thus  continue  to  oppress  the  poor,  they  sin 
also  against  the  Iloly  Spirit,  hecause  they  offend  against  His  very  na-

To  judge  from  the  whole  tone  of  the  Tract,  it  7nust  have  hee7i

hitherto  known  of  the  institute  of  W.''^  itineray-y  preachers,  an  earlier 
date  than  the  year  1382  would  not  suit  this  antagonism.  The  date 
must,  therefore,  remain  uncertain.

XVI. 


DE  DUOBUS  GENERIBUS 
HAERETICORUM. 


BE  DUOBUS   GENERIBUS  HAERETICORUM. 


I 


I.   Contents. 

Two  classes  of  heretics  must  be  driven  out  of  England,  vi%.  the 
Simonists  (popes ,  bishojjs  and  eurates),  and  the  Apostates  (all  the 
priesthood,  especially  the  p>relates)  who  have  lost  almost  all  true  faith, 
and  who  refuse  to  follow  the  lowly  example  of  Ghrist.  —  Now  as  all 
heretics  are  to  be  regarded  as  lepers,  who,  according  to  the  Oospel,  are 
to  dwell  apart,  they  must  be  driven  out,  a7id  whith  them  their  abettors, 
the  clergy,  the  Mendicant  Friars  and  temporal  lords  who  support  them. 
They  can,  indeed,  only  be  expelled  by  a  miracle,  for  the  whole  world 
is  full  of  them. 

II,    Date  of  Composition, 

There  is  no  certain  date  for  fixing  the  time  at  which  this  Tract 
was  written.  With  Arnold,  S.  E.  W.  III,  211,  to  whose  arguments 
I  refer,  I  am  of  opinion  that  it  is  an  early  compilation,  composed 
befwe  1380.  Indeed,  the  grouping  together  of  the  clerus,  the  fratres 
and  the  domini  temporales,  which  never  recurs  in  subsequent  writings, 
and  which  in  fact  would  have  been  impossible  for  W.  at  a  later  period, 
is  in  favour  to  this  view. 

III.   Genuineness, 

This  also  can  scarcely  be  doubted.  The  style  is  troughout  W.^s, 
and  the  position  of  the  treatise  amongst  his  genuine  writings  (compare 


430     J-   WICLIF,  DE  DUOBVS  GENERIBUS  HAJERETICORUM. 

the   old   index    on   the   cover  of  cod.  E)  is  in   favour    of  this.     See 
furtJier : 

(1)  the  Vienna  Widif  Gatalogues,  cp.  above  p.   7 

(2)  Denis,  God.  MS.   Theol.  II,   1443 

(3)  Shirley,  Gatal.  p.  30  No.  96. 

(4)  Leohler,  J.  v.  W.  II.  568. 

The  fragment  is  prohahly  an  extract  from  one  of  W.^s  sermons; 
the  whole  tone  indicates  this  ftota  communitas  etc.  p.  432;  Sed  heu! 
ad  tantum  etc.  p.  432;  Amen  at  the  end);  it  is,  perhaps,  a  2)art  of

Goll.  Gamhr.  B.  16.  2.  fol.  353  —  432  and  G.  123.  fol.  3  —  332).

observanciam  (p.  65:  observancia)  faciendo.  Gompare  also  Arnold,

tance,  as  on  the  one  hand  it  treats,  and  that  with  some  asperity,  of 
the  universal  corruption  of  the  priesthood  (not  tJie  llendicant  Friars)

for  instance,  De  Officio  Pastorali  puhlished  hy  Lechler,  Leipsic  1863, 
and  Mathew,  E.  W.  h.  u.  p.  405  ff.

I,  Division, 

Thesis:  No  private  religion  can  be  equal  to  that  of  which  Ghrist 
is  the  head. 

(a)  Negative  part:    Reputaiion    of  the    opposite    assertions, 

cJiap.  I

the  Mendicant   Orde?'s   more  especiallg  are  injurious  to 
a  true  Ghristian  life,  cliap.    V — VI. 
Gonclusion:  All  Sects  should  he  aholished,  chap.  VI. 

II.    Summary  of  Contents. 

Ckap.  I.  The  Friars  assert  that  their  orders  hold  a  higher  stan- 
dard  of  perfection  than  the  great  Ghurch  i?i  general  founded  hy  Ghrist, 
p.  449.  This  rests  mainly  on  their  suhjective  idea  of  perfectio7i,  p.  450 — 
451.  The  state  of  Ghrist  and  that  of  the  apostles  is  in  reality  a  far 
higher  one,  p.  452.  It  is  a  lie  and  hlasphemy  to  assert  that  Ghrist 
endues  such  as  enter  the  mofiastic  orders  with  especial  grace,  or  that 
on  their  entrance  into  these  orders  they  receive  ahsolution  from  their 
sins,  p.  452 — 453. 

Chap.  11.  All  Sects,  notwithstanding  that  some  good  is  even- 
tually  produced  hy  them,  fall  short  of  Ghrisfs  law,  p.  453 — 455. 
Neither  the  external  marks  of  difference,  nor  the  results  falsely  sup)- 
posed  to  he  attendant  on  the  entrance  into  the  order,  are  sufficient  to 
constitute  a  higher  degree  of  perfection,  p.  456 — 458. 

Chap.  III.  As  examples  pf  the  pernicious  consequences  of  the  Sects^ 
te/iching ,  are  the  two  comhating  Popes,  who  each  claim  ahsolute  per- 
feetion  in  religious    matters   for    their   respective  j)arties,  p.  458,  at

I,  Division, 

Part  I:  Refutation  of  a  general  scholastiG  thesis  (in  ten  Argu- 
ments). 

Part.  II:  Eefutation  of  the  particular  thesis  of  a  Monk  (in  eight 
Argumenis). 

II.   Summary  of  Contents. 

Chap.  I.  Scholastic  refutation  of  the  thesis:  not  every  'private 
religion^  Jias  an  essential  fault.  There  follow  ten  arguments,  also  in 
i-^igid  seholastic  form:  (1)  Every  ^private  religion^  is  erroneous  on 
account  of  its  human  origin;  (2)  it  prevents  the  religious  precepts  of 
the  Gospel  from  being  fulfilled;  (3)  it  rejects  God^s  aid  in  its  Cere- 
monies;  (4)  follows  false  leaders;  (5)  to  choose  it  is  foolish. 

Chap,  II.  (6)  The  solitary  (monastic)  life  itself  is  foolish; 
(7)  it  enforces  obedience  to  man  —  not  to  Christ;  (8)  it  requires  the 
fulfilment  of  commands  beyond  what  is  required  by  general  religion; 
(9)  rests  on  an  imperfect  foundation,  is  originated  by  man,  and  not 
by  Infinite  Wisdom;  (10)  it  pretends  that  it  alone  can  shew  works 
of  true  religion.  From  these  reasons  it  follows  that  the  above  thesis 
is  false,  viz:  every  private  religion  has  a  defectus  essencialis. 

Chap.  III.  The  objections  of  a  reverendus  monachus  to  this 
last  position  are  refuted.  First  Objection:  No  monastic  order  has  such 
defects;  every  monastic  order  is  a  'private  religion%  etc;  Answer  to  this 
proposition.  Second  Objection:  St.  Benedict  has  given  a  complete  and 
universally-admitted  rule,  etc.     Answer  to  this.

inspiration.  Answer.  —  4^^^  Ohjection:  no  private  religion  prevents

I,  Division. 

I.  IntroduGtio7i :   Thesis,  concerning  the  jjaj^al  Citations,  cap.  I. 
II.  Argument: 

(a)   The  arguments  in  favour    of  the   right   of  Citation  are 

untenable  and  sophistical,  cap.  I — IV. 
(h)    The  assumption  of  temporal  power  hy  the  Pope  as  dis- 
played   in    the   right    of  Citationj    is  unjusticahle ,    cap. 
V—VIIL 
III.  Conclusion :   The  Church  should,  therefore,  return  to  the  simple 
Gospel  of  Christ  without  the  Pope  and  his  statutes,  cap.  IX. 

II,   Stmimary  of  Contents. 

Chap.  I.  The  Pope  commits  a  great  wrong  when  he  assumes 
the  right  of  citing  the  King^s  subjects  without  royal  permission,  to 
ap2)ear  at  a  specified  time  and  place,  and  when  he  inflicts  lieavy 
pimishment  for  nonohedience,  p.  546 — 547.  For  he  is  neither  omni- 
scient,  nor  infallihle,  and  places  himself  in  many  cases  in  opposition 
to  God  (for  instance  in  case  of  illness) ,  p.  548.  Neither  Christ 
(Matth.  III;  John  XVIII),  nor  the  Apostles  (St.  Peter  and  Paul)  set 
this  example,  p.  548.  They  came  to  huild  up  the  Church,  not  to  de- 
stroy  it.  There  is  on  the  part  of  the  Pope  no  wish  to  strengthen  the 
faith,  or  to  save  the  souls  of  those  cited;  as  a  rule  it  is  merely  a 
matter  of  administering  punishment,  p.  549 — 550. 

Chap.  II.  The  right  of  Citation  is  generally  derived  either  from 
God,  or  fro7n  the  temporal  Lords,  p.  550.     If  from  God,  where  do

we  find  tvritten  authority  for  it?  j).  550.  If  from  the  temjwral  Lords, 
they  have  (1)  no  right  to  expose  their  subjects  to  the  dangers  of  a 
journey  and  of  foreign  lands,  when  (2)  they  cannot  even  protect  them- 
selves  against  assaults  from  without  and  within,  p.  551.  If,  then,  the 
right  of  Citation  proceed  neither  from  Christ,  nor  from  the  temporal 
Lords,  then  it  comes  from  Satan.  On  the  other  hand,  when  taking 
on  oneself  such  duties,  not  force,  but  voluntary  love  must  prevail. 
The  Citations  however  are  nothing  but  a  forcible  means  of  extorting 
money,  p.  551. 

Chap.  IIL  The  Citations  are  not  only  unfounded  in  Scripture, 
but  are  most  injurious,  (1)  because  the  pilgrims  to  Eome  only  see 
what  is  bad,  p.  552;  (2)  because  the  travellers  are  left  without  spiri-

christ,  who  claims  all  power  over  your  bodies,  as  well  as  your  souls. 
Woe  to  the  land,  which  submits  to  his  supremacy,  p.  553 — 554. 

Chap.  If^.  Enquiry  into  the  three  canonical  grounds  of  excuse, 
necessary  obstacles,  illness,  command  of  the  King,  p.  554 — 555.  W. 
lays  claim  to  these  for  himself,  p.  556. 

Chap.  V.  Notwithstanding  the  pretensions  to  superiority  over 
the  temporal  Lords,  even  over  the  Empteror,  which  contrary  to  Scripture 
are  raised  by  the  Pope  —  himself  a  powerless  fugitive  — ,  the  pious 
Christian  is  unabh  to  obey,  p.  556 — 558. 

Chap,  VI.  If  the  objection  be  raised,  (1)  that  the  Pope  is  the 
Church  as  Peter  once  was,  it  is  to  be  said:  —  only  in  so  far,  as 
like  Peter  he  holds  the  right  faith,  p.  558,  and  does  not  hypocritically 
pretend  to  false  power  etc,  p.  559.  The  true  head  of  the  Church  is 
Christ.  The  Chureh  without  Pope  is  not  therefore  without  head,  but 
is  rather  freed  from  the  oppressive  burden  of  worldly  possessions, 
p.  559. 

Chap.  VIL  If  it  be  objected  (2)  that  through  her  spiritual  power 
Rome  restrains  many  from  sin  and  crime,  this  may  be  admitted  in  a 
certain  sense,  p.  559.  But  with  God  the  question  is  not  'whaV,  but

His  own  hand,  so  that  after  the  removal  of  all  erroneous  human 
additions,  she  may  again  live  in  the  security  of  freedom,  p.  564.

I.  Division. 

L    Inirodttction :  Rom.    VIII,  28,  cap.  I. 

II.  First  division  —  (positive  part)  cap.  I — IV. 

The  Cnisade  is  not  to  be  regarded  as  an  evil  in  every  i^espect, 
it  points 

(a)  to  the  total  perversity  of  popedom  and  its  supporters  (the 
Pope  considered  as  Antichrist),  cap.  I — 11. 

(b)  to  the  bright  future  which  the  Schism  of  the  two  Popes 
has  opened  out  to  the  Church,  cap.  III — IV. 

III.  Second  division  —  (negative  part)  — ;  Objections  raised  against 
a  criticism  of  the  Crusade  (and  their  answers),  cap.    V — X: 

(a)  no  attention  should  be  paid   to    a  few  voices  here  and 

there,  cap.  V — VI, 
{b)  the  pope  has  been  lawfully  chosen  etc,  cap.    VII, 

(c)  Christ  had  endowed  His  Apostles,  therefore  the  Pope  also, 
with  spiritual  power,  cap.    VIII, 

(d)  this  spiritual  grace  is  indispensable   for    the    absolution 
of  sins,  cap.  IX — X. 

IV.  Conclusion:  they  that  take  the  sword,  shall  perish  by  the 
sicord,  cap.  X. 

II,    Summary  of  Contents. 

Chap.  L  All  things  work  together  for  the  good  to  them  that  love 
God;  so  also  the  Crusade  which  is  being  p^eached  to  the  members  of 
fhe  English  Church,  p.  588 ;  for  it  has  exposed  the  Pope^s  hypocrisy 
ind  worldliness;  it  is  not  a  struggle  for  moral  or  religious  rights, 
hut  piirely  for  ivorldly  autliority,  p.  589 — 590. 

Chap,  11.  (1)  It  is  the  task  of  the  civil  authorities  to  maintain 
peace  —  it  becomes  their   duty ,    therefore,    to  remove   the  cause   and

Chap.  III .  The  Crusade  is  the  doing  of  none  other  than  the 
arch  enemy  of  God,  who  for  the  distwbance  of  the  Western  Church 
had  originated  the  sect  of  the  Friars,  p.  597 — 601. 

Chap.  IV.  The  Pope  is  no  longer  the  shepherd  of  the  Church,

VII.   The  Manuscripts. 

(A)  Their  relationship,  (1)  Group  A — E.  That  some  con- 
nection  exists  hetween  these  two  may  he  concliided  (1)  from  the  very 
great  consensus  apparent  in  their  corrupted passages,  cp.  corditer /F";,  47 ; 
20  V,  7;  excog.  VII,  59;  veh.  VII,  58;  Matth.  17  VIII,  17;  ad  ult. 
VIII,  55;  perf.  IX,  27;  ips.  VI,  24;  culp.  VI,  26;  nol.  VI,  29; 
quant.  VIII,  14;  eccl.  (o7n.)  VIII,  69;  idem  IX,  45;  cp.  also  IX, 
42;  45;  —  (2)  from  the  decisive  passages,  such  as  congruit  IX,  46; 
solic.  X,  47;  expurg.  X,  83;  especially  from  sciens  dic.  X,  25  and 
papa  ergo  X,  28;  (3)  from  the  conformity  of  the  marginal  glosses: 
Indulg.  II,  41';  Serg.  III,  3;  No.  tim.  III,  49,  51;  Indulg.  IV,  21; 
Mil.  Chr.  IV,  45;  Nota  mult.  V,  1;  Nota  bell.  V,  34;  Bell.  VI, 
22;  Obed.  VI,  56;  Bell.  VII,  11;  Pugn.  Pape  VII,  46;  Pati  VII, 
62;  Vi.  Chr.  VII,  70;  odis  ve.  vi.  VII,  81,  as  to  this,  cp.  the  cod.; 
Pot.  VIII,  10;  Ele.  Pa.  VIII,  27;  An.  Pa.  mul.  VIII,  32  (with  ref 
to  this,  cp.  the  notes  of  the  other  codd.) ;  Pot.  qu.  hab.  VIII,  39;  Eccl. 
VIII,  45;  Pot.  s.  a.  d.  VIII,  62;  Ind.  VIII,  67;  Sacram.  VIII,  70; 
Absol.  IX,  4;  Conf.  IX,  8;  Absol.  IX,  36;  No.  IX,  44;  Pen.  IX, 
51;  Bell.  X,  2;  Pugn.  Sac.  X,  12;  Glad.  duo  X,  52;  Duo  gl.  X,  90. 
It  is  characteristic  of  these  two  Manuscripts,  (1)  that  the  glosses  are 
at  first  rare,  towards  the  middle  of  the  text  they  suddenly  increase  in 
numher  (from  cap.  VII),  and  then  as  suddenly  decrease  from  cap.  X; 
(2)  that  the  marginals  contained  in  A  and  E  are  not  found  in  the 
other  codices,  and  (3)  the  glosses  of  the  remaining  four  texts  are  quite 
independent  of  these  and  of  each  other.  A  is  not  E^s  original,  cp. 
the  lacuna   in  peccato  et  ad  bellum    etc.  II,  69;    according   to    this

DE  CHRISTO   ET  SUO   ADVERSARIO 
ANTICHRISTO. 


I.  Division. 

I.    hiiroduction:  on  the  unity  of  the  Church,  cap.  I. 
II.    Philosophiml-sGholastic  hasis  of  the  attack,  cap.  I — IV. 
III    The  attack  itself,    V—XV. 

II.    Summary  of  Contents, 

Chap.  I.  The  introduction  starts  fro?n  the  doctrine  of  the  Church. 
AcGording  to  catholic  teaching  the  community  of  the  Elect  is  divided 
into  three  parts :  the  Church  T7'iumphant  (the  hlest  in  Heaven),  the  Church 
Militant  (the  living,  at  war  with  the  world)  and  the  Church  Dormi- 
tant  (those  who  have  fallen  asleep,  i.  e.  the  souls  in  purgatory),  p.  653 — 
654.  These  three  p^ai-ts  must  he  in  harmony ,  if  the  Church  is  to 
flourish.  Hence  the  first  condition  of  healthy  life  is  unity  and  peace 
in  the  ecclesia  militans.  This  unity  is  grounded  on  Exod.  XXV 
and  Ephes.  IV,  p.  654 — 655. 

Chap.  II — If^.  From  the  unity  of  the  ideal  Cliurch  should  spring 
that  of  the  congregation  of  the  faithful,  which  appears  endangered  hy 
the  quatuor  secte  noviter  introducte.  This  fourfold  division  tends 
to  disunion,  p.  656 — 65  7.  The  various  ohjections,  practical,  sophistic 
and  philosophical  are  to  he  set  aside,  p.  658 — 662. 

Chap.  V^.  Having  treated  this  niateria  abstracta,  the  author  jjro- 
ceeds  to  an  examination,  in  polemical  fashion,  of  the  practical  circum- 
stances  of  the  Church,  as  it  then  existed. 


636  INTROBUCTION  TO  JOHN  WICLIF'S 

According  to  apostoUc  doctrim  the  head  of  the  Church  is  Christ: 
in  the  face  of  this  fact  the  Eomish  claims  are  in  every  respect  un- 
justifiahle,  p.  663.  They  come  under  the  four  following  heads:  (1)  Is 
Peter  the  head  of  the  Church?  (Proof  from  Holy  Scripture,  from 
Peter^s  name),  p.  664 — 665. 

Chap.  VJ.  (2)  Is  Peter  the  Vicar  of  Christ,  in  respect  of  having 
a  special  prerogative  ahove  that  of  the  other  disciples  ?  (scriptural  and 
historical  proof),  p.  665 — 668. 

Chap.  J^II.  (3)  Has  the  Eoman  Pontifex  received  his  power  from 
Peter  (scriptural  proof,  with  a  reference  to  history  [Silvester])? 
p.   669—671.  —   Wiclifs  protest,  p.  671. 

Chap.  VIII — IX.  The  lamentahle  division  of  the  Church,  the 
corruption  of  the  clergy ,  the  worldliness  of  the  Pope,  the  incompati- 
hility  of  the  papal  election  hy  the  cardinals  with  holy  Scripture  —  all 
point  to  the  same  truth,  that  the  Church  can  exist  without  the  Pope, 
p.  671—676. 

Chap.  X.  (4)  Is  the  Pope  (in  questions  of  ethics  and  doctrine) 
infallihle?  —  This,  as  well  as  the  three  first  questions,  is  to  he  ans- 
wered  in  the  negative,  p.  677 — 679. 

Chap.  XI.  The  Pope  stands  rather  in  a  position  of  to- 
tal  antagonism  to  Christ:  if  this  thesis  can  he  proved,  he  is  Anti- 
christ.      The  proposition  is  then  demonstrated  in  twelve  cases: 

(1)  Christ  the  truth  —  the  Pope  the  principle  of  false- 
hood  and  lies  (in  words,  writings,  works),  p.  680. 

(2)  Chrisfs  poverty  —  the  Pope^s  wordly  magnificence. 

(3)  Chrisfs  meekness  and  humility  —  the  Pope^s  pride 
and  cruelty  (Crusade),  p.  681 — 682. 

(4)  Chrisfs  law  perfect  and  sufficient  —  the  Pope^s 
new  cruel  law  and  his  oppression  of  the  faithful, 
p.  682—683. 

Chap.  XII.  (5)  Chrisfs  missionary  zeal  and  exhortation  to  missio- 
nary  work  —  the  Pope  and  his  followers  either  en- 
throned  in  gorgeous  palaces,  or  shut  up  in  mona- 
steries,  p.  683 — 685. 

Chap.  XIII.  (6)  Chrisfs  contempt  for  secular  power  —  the  Pope^s 
claim  of  dominion  over  all  earthly  kingdoms,  p.  686. 


BjE  CHBISTO  ET  SUO  ADVHBSABIO  ANTICHBISTO.         637 

(7)  Chrisfs  ohedience  to  the  Einperor  —  the  Pope 
weakens  the  secular  power,  2?.  686. 

(8)  Ghrist  and  this  twelve  simple  disciples  —  the  Pope 
and  his  twelve  crafty,  amhitious,  and  worldly  car- 
dinals,  p)-  686 — 687. 

(9)  Christ  suffered  for  Ris  own  —  the  Pope  exhorts 
to  war,  p.  687 . 

Chap.  XIV.  (10)  Christ  confined  his  mission  to  Judaea  —  the  Pope 
has  emissaries  in  every  land,  hut  only  for  the  sake 
of  power  and  gain,  p.  688. 
(11)  Christ  without  pomp  and  ready  to  serve  —  the 
Pope  has  a  magnificent  court,  and  demands  homage 
even  from  the  Emperor,  p.  689 — 690. 

Chap.  XV.    (12)  Christ  despised  worldly  fame  and  gain  of  gold  — 

everything  is  marketahle  with  the  Pope,  p.  690 — 691.^ 

This,   in  point  of  fact,    is   how  matters  stand.     Conclusion: 

can  the  heliever,   who  desires  to  he  a  disciple  of  Christ,  take  the  Pope 

for  his  example?    Certainly   not,  for  in  this   case  real  following   of 

Christ  would  he  impossihle,  p.  692. 

III,  Date  of  Composition, 

In  the  first  place,  the  whole  tone  of  the  Tract,  which  is  aimed 
against  ihe  Pope,  points,  as  will  he  seen  from  the  review  of  its  con- 
tents,  to  the  later  years  of  Wiclifs  life.  —  But  we  have  hesides  di- 
stinct  references  to  the  douhle  election  to  the  Papacy,  p.  674:  Et  idem 
patet  .  .  .  de  eleccione  erronea  istorum  paparum;  thus  Wiclif  has 
already  at  this  time  rejected  Urhan  VI.,  whom  he  at  first  acknow- 
ledged:^  his  change  of  opinion  dates  apparently  from  Nov.  29,  1378, 
on  which  day  Urhan  issued  the  hulls  for  a  Crusade  against  Cle- 
ment  VII^  —  Moreover  the  residence  of  the  Popes  at  Avignon  and 
Rome  is  implied,  cp.  p.  683  Nam  quidam  papa  etc.  —  Clement  had

1383  or  the  beginning  of  1384  may,  therefore,  be  fixed  upon  with 
tolerable  certainty  as  the  date  of  composition. 

IV.    Geuuineness. 

Upon  this  matter  there  can  hardly  be  the  shadow  of  a  doubt; 
both  internal  and  external  evidence  witness  to  the  authorship  of 
Wiclif. 

Internal  evidence:  the  style,  ideas  and  mode  of  reasoning 
are  throughout  the  same  as  in  the  undoubtedly  genuine  works  of 
Wiclif;  indeed  so  far  does  this  correspondence  extend,  that  particular 
trains  of  thought  in  other  of  Wiclifs  works  are  here  verbally  repro-

II,    Summary  of  Contents. 

Chap.  1.  In  opposition  to  Christ,  the  true  and  mighty  Lord 
of  heaven,  there  stands  a  power  of  the  ahyss,  Antichrist,  who  has  like-

First  Report  of  the  Executive  Committee,  1882-83. 


1.  Furpose  of  the  Society. 

2.  Members,  %  Advance-Subscriptions. 

3.  Manuscripts  copied. 

4.  Booksfor  1882  and  1883. 


5.  Booksfor  1884.    Appealfor  £1000 

for  the  Quincentenary  Publications. 

6.  Thanks  to  Helpers.      Miscellaneous. 

Hon,  Sec.^s  Cash  Account. 


1.  The  "Wyclif  Society  was  founded  in  Marcli,  1882,  "  to 
remove  from  England  the  disgrace  of  having  left  buried 
m  manuscript  the  most  important  v^^orks  of  her  great  early 
Keformer,  John  Wyclif,"  and  to  ensure  that  the  500th 
"anniversary  of  his  death,^  the  year  1884,  should  see  at  work 
a  Society  which  would  keep  on  foot  until  all  his  most  im- 
portant  genuine  writings  should  be  "  given  to  the  world 
through  the  press." 

2.  At  least  300  Members  were  caUed  for  :  230  responded. 
Forty  of  these  were  askt  to  pay  five  years'  subscription  in 
advance,  in  order  that  Manuscripts  might  be  copied,  and 
forty-two  did  so. 

3.  The  foUowing  Treatises  have  been  copied,  those  starred 
(*),  whoUy ;  those  daggered  (t),  partly ;  (the  numbers  are 
those  of  Shirley's  Catalogue)  : — 

*11.    De  Actibus  Animae  (in  Shirley  :  De  Anima). 

tl2.    De  Incamatione  Verbi  (all  the  Oriel  MS.  :  part  of  the 

Vienna  MS.). 
*i4.    De  Dominio  Divino.     (In  three  books.)

or  how  best  to  get  the  WycHf  Society  its  £1000  towards  printing  WYCLIF'S 
Works,  should  write  to  the  Hon.  Sec,  Mr.  J.  W.  Standerwick.  The  Luther 
Comraemoration  Coramittee  will  help  in  the  Quincentenary  arrangements.  WycHf 
diedon  Dec.  31,  1384.

Commissions  have  been  given  for  tlie  copying  of  tlie  rest 
of  tlie  Summa  (namely  Books  X.  and  XI.,  De  Simonia  and 
De  Apostasia),  and  of  all  Wyclif^s  other  Latin  works  except 
the  Philosopliical  ones  and  the  Sermons. 

4.  Tlie  work  of  the  first  copiers  employed  was  not  satis- 
factory,  and  the  Committee  f ound  that  there  was  no  chance 
of  producing  any  independent  Society  book  till  1884.  They 
therefore  arranged  with  Dr.  Rudolf  Buddensieg,  of  Dresden, 
— whose  appeal  to  English  students  had  in  great  measure 
led  to  the  foundation  of  the  Society — that  the  edition  of 
Wyclif^s  Polemical  Works,  which  he  had  undertaken  in 
Germany,  should  be  issued  also  here,  with  an  English  Intro- 
duction,  Notes,  etc,  as  the  Society's  first  Publication,  vol.  i. 
for  1882,  and  vol.  ii.  for  1883,  each  volume  consisting  of  about 
600  pages.  This  work,  the  arrangement  of  which  is,  of 
course,  after  the  German  manner,  is  now  ready,  and  contains 
— ^besides  a  very  valuable  appreciative  account  of  Wyclif 
and  his  work,  critical  apparatus,  a  list  of  the  Yienna  MSS., 
and  fuU  Index — the  foUowing  twenty-six  Polemical  Tracts 
(Shirley's  numbers  are  added)  : — 

A, — Against  the  Sects. 
De  Fundatione  Sectarum.     (91.) 
De  Ordinatione  Fratrum.    Shirlej's  (84)  De  Concordatione  Fratrum 

cum  secta  simplici  Christi,  sive  De  Sectis  Monachorum.    In 

four  chapters.

De  Nova  Prsevaricantia  Mandatorum.  In  eight  chapters.  ('  A  very 
interesting  Tract  against  the  Regnlars,  written  after  the  Great 
Schism  of  the  West,'  a.d.  1378.)  (79.)  Shirley's  '  31 .  De  Purga- 
torio '  is  part  of  this  Treatise. 

De  Triplici  Vinculo  Amoris.     In  ten  chapters.     (49.) 

De  Septem  Donis  Spiritus  Sancti.     In  9  chapters.    (27.) 

De  Quatuor  Sectis  Novellis.  (1.  The  Priests  endowed  with  lands 
and  lordships  ;  2.  The  landed  Monastic  Orders  ;  3.  The  Canons  ; 
4.  The  BeggiDg  Friars.)    (85.) 

Purgatorium  sectse  Christi,  sive  contra  Religiones  Privatas, 
Ashburnham  MS.  xxvii.  c.  fF.  49-54.  This  is  not  in  Shirley's 
Catalogue.   It  is  an  exhortation  to  put  down  the  sects  of  Friars. 

De  Novis  Ordinibus.     In  three  chapters.    (87.)

tibus  (against  the  boasting  of  the  Franciscans).     (78.)

English,  Shirley,  No.  59,  p.  48.  Printed  in  Arnold,  iii.,  242.)  (74.) 
Cruciata.     Shirley's  75.    Contra  Cruciatam  Papae.    In  nine  chapters. 

(On  the  Crusade  of  the  rival  Popes  against  each  other  during

Popes  and  Friars.)     (83.) 
Quatuor  Imprecationes.     (Four  conclusions  about  the  state  of  the

The  two  volumes,  witli  binding,  etc.,  will  cost  about  £280  ; 
and  in  order  to  pay  tbis  sum,  tbe  Subscriptions  for  1883  are 
wanted  at  once. 

The  Committee  hope  to  add  to  the  issue  of  1883,  Wyclif^s 
De  Incarnatione  Verbi,  now  at  press,  edited  from  the  Yienna 
and  Oriel  MSS.  by  the  Eev.  Edward  Harris,  M.A.  But 
until  the  1883  Subscriptions  come  in,  no  decision  can  be 
arrived  at  about  the  issue  of  books.  A  sum  of  £200  is  still 
wanted  for  copying  and  other  non-printing  expenses.     Of 


4     §  5.  Worksfor  1884,  d^c.    The  £1000  Quincentenary  Fund. 

tlie  Society^s  small  income,  only  about  £150  a  year  is  available 
for  printing,  and  this  means  only  one  volume  a  year.  (To 
prevent  any  lowering  of  price  of  the  Society's  books,  tbe 
number  printed  is  limited  to  500,  of  whicli  50  are  given 
to  the  Editor  of  each  Text.^) 

5.  For  1884,  the  first  volume  (Books  i  and  ii)  of  the  De 
Civili  Dominio  is  at  press,  edited  by  Heginald  Lane  Poole, 
M.A.,  Oxford. 

Mr.  F.  D.  Matthew  has  nearly  ready  for  press  the  De 
Mandatis  Dei  {Divinis,  Shirley)  and  De  Statu  Linocentiae. 

Dr.  BuDDENSiEG  is  preparing  for  press  the  De  Veritate 
Sanctm  8eripturm. 

Prof .  LosERTH  of  Czernowitz  has  in  hand  the  De  JScclesia, 
and  Mr.  Poole  the  De  Dominio  Divino. 

Mr.  J.  H.  Hessels  of  Cambridge  is  preparing  the  De 
Actibus  Animce ;  but  it  is  a  very  difficult  treatise,  and  he 
wishes  to  give  it  the  time  necessary  for  a  satisfactory  under- 
standing  of  the  scholastic  philosophy  involved  in  it. 

Now  if  the  Members  of  the  Society  will  only  bestir  them- 
selves  and  raise  £1000  for  the  Quincentenary  of  Wyclif's 
death,  all  these  works,  and  more,  can  be  printed  and  issued 
next  year.  The  truest  honour  that  can  be  paid  to  Wyclif's 
memory,  is  to  print  his  words,  the  records  of  his  thoughts, 
which,  to  the  disgrace  of  every  Englishman,  have  been 
left  unheeded  in  foreign  libraries  for  now  five  hundred 
years.  The  monument  *  aere  perennius,'  which  Germany  is 
now  erecting  to  the  memory  of  her  Luther,  is  a  new  critical 
edition  of  Luther's  Works,  of  which  the  first  volume  was 
issued  on  the  day  of  the  Luther  Centenary,  November  10, 
1883.  And  till  all  our  great  Peformer's  most  important 
Treatises  are  in  print,  no  question  of  monument  or  other 
memorial  to  him  need  be  raised.  The  Committee  therefore 
repeat  from  the  Society's  Prospectus  their  "appeal  to  all 
who  care  for  the  Peligion,  the  Freedom,  the  Language,  and 
the  History  of  England,  for  aid  in  the  work  they  have 
undertaken.  No  party  feeling  whatever  enters  into  the 
Society's  plan.  The  only  desire  is,  to  do  England's  long- 
neglected  duty  to  the  memory  of  a  great  English  Worthy." 

6.  The  Committee  wish  to  express  their  thanks,  and  those 
of  the  Society,  to  Dr.  Buddensieg  for  his  admirable  edition

amouut  necessary  for  that  purpose.
